title: Multi-Agent Security: Architecture Matters More Than You Think
summary: This paper presents the first systematic empirical study of how architectural decisions in multi-agent systems (MAS) affect the tradeoff between task performance and security. Across three environments and 13 configurations, the authors find that MAS designs are generally more vulnerable than single agents, with attack success rates varying by up to 3.8x depending on architecture choices like agent roles, communication topology, and memory design.
extractedSignals: Architectural security must become a first-class design consideration for multi-agent systems, as no single configuration is universally safe and the attack surface expands dramatically with coordination complexity.

For To Play Claw users building production multi-agent systems, this research provides critical evidence that security cannot be assumed from individual agent robustness alone. The findings directly impact how developers should evaluate and select agent architectures, communication patterns, and memory designs for their specific use cases.
Multi-agent architectures introduce unique attack surfaces that don't exist in single-agent settings, even when individual agents are secure
Agent roles (hierarchical vs. flat), communication topology (broadcast vs. point-to-point), and memory design (shared vs. private) each significantly impact security posture
Developers must evaluate security alongside task performance when choosing MAS architectures, as the optimal design varies by environment and threat model
